questions.question: Redis vs Memcached vs Caffeine vs Hazelcast — which cache for what?
questions.title: Redis vs Memcached vs Caffeine vs Hazelcast
questions.direct_answer: Different problems. **Caffeine** is a local, in-process cache for a single JVM — nanosecond access, no network. Use for hot data that each instance can keep independently. **Memcached** is a distributed, in-memory KV store that's simple and fast but feature-thin — just strings, no persistence, no replication, no data structures. **Redis** is Memcached plus everything: rich data types (lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes, streams), persistence, replication, cluster mode, Lua scripting, pub/sub, modules. **Hazelcast** is a distributed data grid with near-caching, compute, and transactions — more than a cache, closer to in-memory computing. **Default choice in 2026: Caffeine for local L1 + Redis for shared L2.** Memcached is niche (legacy or pure KV at massive scale); Hazelcast for enterprises that want compute and cache together.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding cache topologies, Redis feature depth, when each tool fits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating Redis as just a KV store; missing local+shared two-tier pattern; picking Memcached when Redis features matter
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss two-tier caching, cache-aside vs read-through, consistency invalidation, Redis Cluster vs Sentinel, Caffeine sizing with Window TinyLFU

sections.title: Four Caches, Four Problems
sections.content:
Caching is not a single problem. Four distinct tools solve four distinct layers:

**Caffeine** — Java in-process cache (successor to Guava Cache). Lives in the JVM heap. Nanosecond access. No network. Window TinyLFU admission policy gives near-optimal hit rate. Perfect for hot data that each service instance can hold (config, feature flags, hot lookup tables, per-request memoization). Limit: every instance has its own copy; no shared state.

**Memcached** — the original distributed in-memory KV. Simple protocol (SET/GET/INCR). Strings only. No persistence, no replication, no data structures. Horizontally scalable via client-side sharding. Operationally trivial. Use when you need pure KV at massive scale and don't need anything Redis offers. Most new systems in 2026 pick Redis instead.

**Redis** — Memcached plus rich data structures plus persistence plus replication plus Cluster plus Lua plus pub/sub plus modules. Strings, lists, hashes, sets, sorted sets, streams, bitmaps, HyperLogLog, geospatial, JSON (module), search (module), time-series (module). Not just a cache — often used as a feature store, rate limiter, session store, leaderboard, queue, pub/sub broker. Single-threaded command execution (fast; predictable; no locks). Redis 7+ adds multithreaded I/O. Default cache in 2026.

**Hazelcast** — distributed in-memory data grid. Near caches + distributed maps + compute + transactions + SQL. Java-first (was IMDG standard). Strong in enterprise Java. Competes with Redis Enterprise, Apache Ignite, Infinispan.

**Two-tier caching is the norm in 2026.**
- **L1 (in-process)**: Caffeine for per-instance hot data; µs access; no network
- **L2 (distributed)**: Redis for shared state across instances; ms access; durable

This reduces Redis traffic 10–50× while keeping shared consistency.

sections.title: Feature Comparison
sections.content:
| Feature | Caffeine | Memcached | Redis | Hazelcast |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Topology** | In-process (JVM) | Distributed | Distributed | Distributed |
| **Access latency** | ~100ns | ~0.5ms | ~0.5ms | ~0.5–1ms |
| **Data types** | Object refs (Java) | Strings only | Rich (list, hash, set, sorted set, stream, JSON) | Rich (map, queue, set, list, topic) |
| **Persistence** | No | No | RDB snapshot + AOF log | Optional (file, MapStore) |
| **Replication** | No | No | Async/semi-sync | Async/sync |
| **Clustering** | N/A | Client sharding | Redis Cluster (16384 slots) | Built-in |
| **Eviction** | Window TinyLFU, size, TTL | LRU | LRU, LFU, TTL per key | LRU, LFU, TTL |
| **Pub/Sub** | No | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Scripting** | N/A | No | Lua, Functions | Entry processors, distributed tasks |
| **Transactions** | No | CAS (limited) | MULTI/EXEC + WATCH | ACID |
| **Language** | Java only | Any client | Any client | Java primary, other clients |
| **Memory limit** | Heap | RAM per node | RAM per node | RAM across nodes |
| **Consistency** | N/A | Single-node per key | Strong per node, async replica | Strong or eventual, configurable |
| **Typical use** | L1 cache, per-JVM hot data | Legacy KV | L2 cache, feature store, queue, rate-limit | Enterprise grid, cache + compute |
| **Operational cost** | Trivial | Low | Medium (Cluster, failover) | Medium-high |

sections.title: Decision Framework
sections.content:
**Start with the access pattern:**

**Pattern 1: Per-instance hot data** — small, rarely changes, OK if each instance has own copy
- Examples: feature flags, config, country list, currency rates
- → **Caffeine** (in-process, zero network)

**Pattern 2: Shared cache across instances** — most web / API caching
- Examples: user session, product page HTML, computed result reused by all instances
- → **Redis** (shared, fast, rich features)

**Pattern 3: Both** — hot data needs local speed; invalidation/consistency shared
- → **Caffeine (L1) + Redis (L2)** with invalidation via Redis pub/sub

**Pattern 4: Pure KV at massive scale, no features needed**
- → **Memcached** or Redis (Redis usually still wins for familiarity + feature headroom)

**Pattern 5: Enterprise grid with compute and transactions**
- → **Hazelcast**, **Apache Ignite**, or **Infinispan**

**Redis-specific sub-choices:**

- **Redis Standalone** — single node; backups via RDB/AOF; no HA
- **Redis Sentinel** — master + replicas + Sentinel processes for failover; single shard
- **Redis Cluster** — horizontal partitioning across 16384 hash slots; auto failover
- **Redis Enterprise / ElastiCache Redis / Memorystore / Upstash** — managed offerings

**When to use Redis for non-cache roles:**
- **Rate limiter**: `INCR` + `EXPIRE`; sliding window via sorted sets
- **Distributed lock**: `SET NX PX` + Lua for unlock; consider Redlock for multi-node safety
- **Session store**: hash per session; TTL for expiry
- **Leaderboard**: sorted set; `ZADD`/`ZREVRANGE`
- **Queue / stream**: Lists or Streams (richer, with consumer groups)
- **Pub/Sub**: simple fan-out (not durable; use Streams for durable)
- **Feature store**: hashes keyed by entity; low-latency reads for ML

**When Caffeine is worth it:**
- Called very frequently (> 10K calls/sec/instance)
- Computation is expensive (DB hit, external call)
- Data has locality / repetition
- Inconsistency window of seconds to minutes is acceptable

**Caffeine sizing:**
- Size by entry count (maximumSize) or heap weight (maximumWeight)
- Start with 10k–100k entries; tune via hit rate metrics
- TTL (expireAfterWrite) often more useful than LRU alone
- Use Caffeine's `recordStats()` and expose via Micrometer

**Redis sizing:**
- Monitor memory; set `maxmemory` + eviction policy (`allkeys-lru`, `volatile-lru`, `allkeys-lfu`)
- Plan 30–50% headroom for fragmentation, replication buffers
- Cluster mode for > 100GB working set or > 100K ops/sec per shard
- Beware big keys (> 1MB) and hot keys (single key with > 10K ops/sec)

sections.title: Trade-offs and Gotchas
sections.content:
**Caffeine: stale data per instance.** Each instance independent; invalidation requires pub/sub or short TTL. Acceptable for short-TTL / eventually-consistent data; dangerous for quotas or counters.

**Caffeine heap pressure.** Unbounded or large caches cause GC. Always set `maximumSize` / `maximumWeight`. Monitor with `recordStats()`.

**Memcached feature ceiling.** No persistence; restart = cold cache. No data structures; everything is strings. Client-side sharding = rebalancing pain. In 2026, most new projects pick Redis by default.

**Redis single-threaded per shard.** One expensive command (`KEYS *`, big `SMEMBERS`) blocks everything. Use `SCAN`, avoid big keys, shard hot keys. Redis 7 has multi-threaded I/O but commands still single-threaded.

**Redis persistence trade-offs.**
- **RDB**: fast restart, point-in-time snapshot; lose recent writes
- **AOF**: near-durable (fsync every second); slower restart, bigger files
- For cache, often disable persistence; warm from source on restart
- For 'database-ish' use, AOF + RDB both

**Redis Cluster complexity.** Multi-key operations limited to same hash slot; `MULTI/EXEC` requires same-slot keys; use hash tags `{user:42}:*`. Client needs to know topology (smart clients).

**Distributed locks are hard.** Single-node `SET NX PX` is safe *within one Redis*. Redlock (multiple masters) adds complexity and is debated (Kleppmann critique). For many apps, DB row lock or advisory lock is simpler.

**Cache invalidation is hard.** The two hard problems in CS. Common patterns:
- **TTL only** — simplest; stale for TTL window
- **Write-through** — write to cache + DB; stale risk if cache failure ignored
- **Cache-aside with explicit invalidate** — on write, delete key; next read misses and reloads
- **Pub/sub invalidation** — for L1+L2, publish invalidate message; all L1s evict key
- **Event-driven** — DB CDC → invalidation events

**Thundering herd.** Key expires, 1000 requests hit DB simultaneously. Fix: request coalescing / singleflight (Caffeine does this natively); probabilistic early expiration; mutex per key.

**Redis is not a database.** Tempting because of features, but durability is weaker than Postgres. For durable source of truth, use Redis alongside (not instead of) a real DB. Exceptions: specific high-write workloads (rate limit counters) where loss tolerance exists.

**Hazelcast footprint.** Heavier than Redis; Java-centric; less multi-language support. Strong for Java shops that need grid + compute. Less popular in microservices world; Redis dominates.

**Memcached vs Redis in 2026:**
- Memcached still shines at ultra-high-throughput pure KV (Facebook scale)
- For 99% of teams, Redis is better default
- ElastiCache supports both; Upstash/Memorystore favor Redis

**Cost at scale.**
- Caffeine: free (just Java heap)
- Redis (managed): ~$30–150/GB/month depending on provider and tier
- Memcached (managed): similar to Redis
- Hazelcast Enterprise: licensed

**Multi-region caching.** Redis Enterprise Active-Active (CRDT-based); local Redis per region + eventual consistency. Writes replicate; latency varies. Complex; only when truly needed.

**Observability signals to watch:**
- **Hit rate** (L1 and L2 separately)
- **Latency p50/p99**
- **Memory used / maxmemory**
- **Evictions/sec**
- **Connected clients**
- **Commands/sec per type**
- **Replica lag**
- **Big key / hot key detection**

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Caffeine = local L1** (in-process Java, nanosecond); **Redis = shared L2** (distributed, rich features)
- **Two-tier (Caffeine + Redis)** is the 2026 default for high-throughput apps
- **Memcached** is feature-thin; Redis is default for new systems unless pure-KV extreme scale
- **Redis is more than a cache** — rate limiter, session store, leaderboard, feature store, queue, pub/sub
- **Redis is single-threaded per shard** — avoid `KEYS *`, big keys, hot keys
- **Redis Cluster** for > 100GB or > 100K ops/sec per shard; otherwise Sentinel or standalone
- **Caffeine TinyLFU** admission gives near-optimal hit rate; bound size/TTL
- **Hazelcast** for enterprise grid with compute; less common in modern microservices
- **Cache invalidation is hard** — TTL, write-through, pub/sub invalidation, or CDC
- **Redis is not a durable database** — combine with Postgres/DynamoDB for source of truth

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
These solve different problems.

**Caffeine**
- In-process Java cache
- Lives in JVM heap; nanosecond access; no network
- Window TinyLFU admission policy; near-optimal hit rate
- Per-instance copy; each instance independent
- Use for hot data each instance can hold: config, feature flags, hot lookup tables

**Memcached**
- Original distributed in-memory KV
- Simple: strings only, no persistence, no replication, no data structures
- Client-side sharding
- Horizontally scalable, operationally trivial
- In 2026, most new systems pick Redis instead

**Redis**
- Memcached plus everything: rich data structures (list, hash, set, sorted set, stream)
- Persistence (RDB + AOF), replication, Cluster mode, Lua, pub/sub, modules
- Single-threaded command execution; fast and predictable
- Not just a cache: rate limiter, session store, leaderboard, queue, feature store
- Default in 2026 for distributed cache

**Hazelcast**
- Distributed in-memory data grid
- Near caches + distributed maps + compute + transactions + SQL
- Java-first; strong in enterprise Java
- Competes with Redis Enterprise, Apache Ignite, Infinispan

**Two-tier caching is the 2026 default**
- L1 Caffeine: per-instance hot data; microsecond access; no network
- L2 Redis: shared state across instances; millisecond access; durable
- Reduces Redis traffic 10 to 50x while keeping shared consistency

**Decision framework**
- Per-instance hot data, small, rarely changes: Caffeine
- Shared cache across instances: Redis
- Both: Caffeine L1 plus Redis L2 with pub/sub invalidation
- Pure KV at massive scale, no features: Memcached or Redis
- Enterprise grid with compute: Hazelcast or Ignite

**Redis sub-choices**
- Standalone: single node, backups, no HA
- Sentinel: master + replicas + Sentinel failover
- Cluster: horizontal partition across 16384 hash slots
- Managed: ElastiCache, Memorystore, Upstash, Redis Enterprise

**When Redis does more than cache**
- Rate limiter: INCR plus EXPIRE; sliding window via sorted sets
- Distributed lock: SET NX PX; consider Redlock for multi-node safety
- Session store: hash per session; TTL
- Leaderboard: sorted set
- Queue / stream: Lists or Streams with consumer groups
- Pub/Sub: fan-out, not durable
- Feature store: hashes keyed by entity for ML

**Trade-offs and gotchas**

*Caffeine stale data per instance*
- Each instance independent; invalidation requires pub/sub or short TTL
- Acceptable for short-TTL data; dangerous for counters or quotas

*Caffeine heap pressure*
- Always set maximumSize or maximumWeight
- Monitor with recordStats

*Redis single-threaded per shard*
- One expensive command (KEYS *, big SMEMBERS) blocks everything
- Use SCAN, avoid big keys, shard hot keys

*Redis persistence*
- RDB: fast restart, point-in-time; lose recent writes
- AOF: near-durable; slower restart, bigger files
- For cache, often disable persistence; warm from source

*Redis Cluster complexity*
- Multi-key operations limited to same hash slot
- Use hash tags like {user:42}:*
- Client needs topology awareness (smart clients)

*Distributed locks are hard*
- SET NX PX is safe within one Redis; Redlock is debated
- DB row lock or advisory lock often simpler

*Cache invalidation is hard*
- TTL only: simplest; stale for TTL window
- Write-through: write cache plus DB; stale risk if cache fails
- Cache-aside with explicit invalidate: on write, delete key
- Pub/sub invalidation for L1+L2
- CDC-driven for event-based invalidation

*Thundering herd*
- Key expires; 1000 requests hit DB
- Fix: request coalescing / singleflight (Caffeine does this natively)
- Probabilistic early expiration; mutex per key

*Redis is not a database*
- Durability weaker than Postgres
- Use alongside, not instead of, a real DB
- Exceptions: specific high-write workloads where loss tolerance exists

**Cost at scale**
- Caffeine: free
- Redis managed: $30 to 150/GB/month depending on provider
- Hazelcast Enterprise: licensed

**Observability signals to watch**
- Hit rate (L1 and L2 separately)
- Latency p50/p99
- Memory used / maxmemory
- Evictions/sec
- Connected clients
- Commands/sec per type
- Replica lag
- Big key / hot key detection

**The strategic answer**
- Caffeine is local L1; Redis is shared L2
- Two-tier is the 2026 default
- Memcached is feature-thin; Redis wins for new systems
- Redis is more than a cache: rate limiter, session, leaderboard, queue, feature store
- Single-threaded per shard; avoid big/hot keys
- Cache invalidation is genuinely hard; design it carefully
- Redis is not a durable database; combine with Postgres or DynamoDB
